claims.text: Protective oxide development and retention are governed by formation of a stable oxide layer.
The protective oxide layer grows slowly.
Synergistic effects among multiple principal elements promote oxide-layer formation.
Synergistic effects among multiple principal elements improve oxide-layer adhesion.
Exposure above 800°C in an oxidizing atmosphere forms an oxide layer on the alloy surface.
The multicomponent nature of high-entropy alloys promotes formation of a complex oxide layer.
The multicomponent nature of high-entropy alloys promotes formation of a stable oxide layer.
The resulting oxide layer adheres well to the alloy substrate.
A stable, adherent oxide layer provides oxidation resistance.
The high-entropy alloy will develop and retain a protective oxide layer.
The high-entropy alloy will exhibit superior oxidation resistance to conventional Ni-based or Co-based alloys under the same conditions.
The hypothesis applies from 800°C to 1200°C in air or oxygen-rich environments.
The exact compositions and processing conditions that optimize oxide formation and adhesion are not well understood.
Oxide thickness, oxide adhesion strength, and oxidation-induced weight gain can be compared between high-entropy and conventional alloys.

contradictions.description: The conditions require temperatures above 800°C, whereas the boundary includes 800°C itself.
